Animosity means a strong, active feeling of hostility or bitter dislike toward someone or something. It is not just a quiet, passive feeling of not liking someone — it carries a sense of real tension, bitterness, and opposition that you can almost feel in the air between people.

Think of it this way: if you simply don't like a flavor of ice cream, that is just a preference. But if two neighbors have been in a loud, bitter feud for years, each one glaring at the other and going out of their way to make the other's life difficult — that is animosity.

Several things make animosity stand out from ordinary words like "dislike" or "displeasure":

It is intense. Animosity sits well above mild dislike on the emotional scale. It is a deep, burning kind of hostility, not a passing irritation. If someone cuts you off in traffic and you feel briefly annoyed, that is not animosity. But if a colleague has been sabotaging your work for two years and you feel a burning resentment every time you see them, that is closer to animosity.

It is active, not passive. A person who feels animosity toward someone doesn't just quietly avoid them. The feeling is charged — it tends to push outward. It often shows in tone of voice, body language, sharp words, or deliberate actions against the other person.

It is often mutual. Animosity frequently exists between two parties, not just in one direction. Two rival companies, two old friends who had a falling-out, two political groups — animosity often burns on both sides.

It has roots. Animosity is rarely random. It usually grows out of a conflict, a betrayal, a long history of tension, or a clash of values. There is almost always a reason behind it, even if it has grown far bigger than the original cause.

These examples will show you how the word works in real life:

  • "There was clear animosity between the two candidates during the debate — they barely looked at each other."
  • "She smiled politely, but her animosity toward him was obvious to everyone in the room."
  • "Years of unfair treatment had built up a deep animosity in the workers toward the management."
  • "The animosity between the two rival gangs made the neighborhood feel unsafe."
  • "He claimed he felt no animosity toward his former business partner, but his actions told a different story."
  • "The peace talks were difficult because of the long-standing animosity between the two nations."
How It Compares to Similar Words

Since you want to truly master this word, it helps to know how it sits among its neighbors:

Dislike is the mildest. You dislike a TV show, a food, or a habit. It is low-energy and largely personal.

Hostility is close to animosity but leans more toward behavior — hostile actions, a hostile tone. Animosity is more about the internal feeling that drives that behavior.

Enmity is very close to animosity and is often used interchangeably. However, enmity tends to sound slightly more formal and can feel more permanent and deep-rooted — like the enmity between two ancient kingdoms. Animosity can be strong but still feel more like something that exists right now in a specific situation.

Hatred is the most extreme. Hatred is an all-consuming, overwhelming feeling. Animosity is very strong but still below the level of pure hatred. You might feel animosity toward a difficult boss; you might feel hatred toward someone who has deeply wronged you in a life-altering way.

So the rough scale looks like: dislike → hostility → animosity → enmity → hatred.

Certain words are very commonly paired with animosity. Knowing these will help you recognize and use the word naturally:

  • "harbor animosity" — to quietly hold onto a feeling of animosity inside you ("She harbored animosity toward her sister for years.")
  • "bear animosity toward" — similar to harbor, it means to carry that feeling ("He bore no animosity toward anyone who disagreed with him.")
  • "deep-seated animosity" — animosity that is rooted very deeply, often from a long time ago
  • "personal animosity" — hostility that is specifically between two individuals, not groups
  • "animosity between" — highlights that the feeling exists on both sides ("the animosity between the two teams")
  • "racial/political/religious animosity" — animosity that exists between groups based on identity or beliefs
The Register: When and Where People Use This Word

Animosity is a semi-formal to formal word. You will find it often in news articles, books, academic writing, political speeches, and thoughtful conversation. It is not a word people usually use in casual everyday chat — you would rarely hear someone say "I've got animosity toward my neighbor" in a casual text. In everyday speech, people tend to say "I can't stand him" or "there's bad blood between them."

However, when you write — in essays, emails, reports, or formal pieces — using "animosity" instead of vague phrases like "bad feelings" makes your language far more precise and powerful.
If you ever need to recall this word in a flash: animosity = strong, active, bitter hostility between people or groups, rooted in conflict or tension, and stronger than simple dislike.
